item.title: @SemiconductorsX：韩国官方报告显示至2030年三星与SK海力士半导体工厂面临逾26万名建筑劳动力缺口
item.description:
Samsung and SK Hynix semiconductor plants need over 260,000 extra workers by 2030. The people are not there.

The Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport said on the 24th that large factory builds plus housing targets are tightening construction labor. It formed a public-private consultative body that includes Samsung C&T, SK Ecoplant, Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and major partners. Piping, welding and duct work are the tightest trades. Semiconductor sites demand higher skill than ordinary construction. Precision piping needs one to two years of field experience. Companies that train workers still lose them to other sites.

Housing adds pressure. The government aims to start more than 1.5 million capital-area homes between this year and 2030. Existing crews can shift to semiconductor projects and leave housing short. Construction labor is already aging. Workers in their 50s and 60s make up 63% of the domestic workforce. Youth inflows remain low.

Samsung is expanding Pyeongtaek P5. Six more fabs are planned in the Yongin advanced system semiconductor complex. SK Hynix is building the first of four fabs in its Yongin cluster. The Honam mega-project adds two fabs each for Samsung and SK Hynix, with groundwork starting next year and mass production targeted for 2030.

The ministry plans joint training so finished workers can move straight onto sites. It will also try to pull in idle skilled workers and retired soldiers.

How much of the 260,000 shortfall gets filled before the Yongin and Honam cleanrooms need full crews?

item.title: 【回复】@sgl_project：SGLang团队发布关于百度ERNIE 5.5 Flash解码加速实现原理的深度解析
item.description:
回复 @sgl_project
Congrats to @Baidu_ERNIE on releasing ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview! SGLang is proud to power day-0 serving support.

It's a 280B sparse MoE with 14B activated per token, a 1M context window, and reasoning, tool calling and a DSpark speculative draft built in.

Together with the Baidu ERNIE team, we pushed BS=1 decoding from 102 to 1,074 tok/s on 4 Blackwell GPUs (55K in / 1K out, simulated DSpark acceptance length 5.5). With block size 7 it reaches ~1,310 tok/s.

How we got there: TP instead of DP/EP for both attention and MoE, W4A8 routed experts, a MegaLLMoE megakernel that runs a whole MoE layer in one launch, One-Pass mHC, and communication fused straight into the compute kernels.

The core kernels are open-sourced in HALOps, and FP4 / FP8 / BF16 recipes are in the cookbook.

Blog and cookbook in the comments👇

Thanks for the question. The 30% number doesn't line up with what NVIDIA reports.

The Singapore figure people point to was a billing number, not a shipping number. Under the old reporting, Singapore was about 18% of fiscal 2025 revenue and 21-22% in the first half of fiscal 2026. But NVIDIA said shipments to Singapore were under 2% of revenue, and that over 99% of the controlled data center compute billed there was for US-based customers. It was mostly where large US customers send their invoices.

Late last year NVIDIA switched to reporting revenue by where the customer is headquartered and recast prior years. On that basis China, including Hong Kong, peaked at about 19% of revenue in fiscal 2025, was about 9% for fiscal 2026, and about 8% in the July quarter. Licensed Hopper sales to China in the October quarter were $2.4 billion, about 2% of revenue, and they are already out of the guide.

Why we don't see it as the main issue: NVIDIA is still supply constrained, so parts that can't go to China get sold to someone else, and management raised next year's growth outlook to about 75% after the new export rules came out.

The part of the bear case we take seriously is the offshore angle. If Chinese demand was being served through Southeast Asian neoclouds and the new rules shut that off, that capacity comes back to market. In a tight year it gets absorbed. It shows up when supply loosens, which is 2028, and that is the same window where we already moved our view toward risk. item.title: @fchollet：François Chollet发文探讨智能系统的两类适应时间尺度
item.description:
All intelligent systems I've ever seen have exactly two adaptation timescales.

The first one is on-the-fly situation modeling. In humans, this is known as fluid intelligence. In modern AI, this is implemented via reasoning chain generation or program generation.

The second one is offline mining of a long buffer of past experiences to extract the reusable abstractions that enable on-the-fly situation modeling. In humans, this is known as long-term plasticity or connectome learning. In modern AI, this is pre-training and post-training.

Up until late 2024, AI only had the second phase -- no fluid intelligence, only storage and retrieval of patterns seen at training time.

(slide from a recent talk I gave at Berkeley)

item.title: 【回复】@sh_reya：研究发现小型大语言模型在成对比较任务中存在明显的顺序偏置与不稳定性
item.description:
回复 @sh_reya
New lab blog post! How do you run complex semantic top-k queries on your unstructured text, accurately and at scale? E.g., "which sales calls most clearly show a customer committing to buy?"

Common convention is to (1) use pairwise LLM comparisons for accuracy (e.g., "does call A show more commitment to buy than call B?"), since cosine similarity on off-the-shelf embeddings misses nuanced criteria, and (2) use small LLMs, so it's cheap at scale.

Surprisingly, we find that just asking the small LLM to score each record and sorting (a "pointwise" approach) is just as accurate (if not more) on a few business-oriented top-k tasks, and up to 13x faster in our experiments.
原帖

回复 @sh_reya
Why does pairwise do worse? Interestingly, if you swap the order of the two records in the prompt, many small LLMs pick a different record! Qwen3-0.6B basically never picks the same one; bigger models are more consistent, but even the best one we tried (Jev) still flips on a whopping 12% of pairs in one dataset!

item.title: @rauchg：Rauchg评论Vercel Board及代理协作架构理念
item.description:
An actually good board!

@mattpocockuk：Vercel Board has been lighting my brain on fire for the last few days

It's a genius idea, but I think most teams should build it from scratch

Basically just a private Slack workspace for your agents AND developers (which can even sync to Slack channels for better observability)

The idea (not necessarily Vercel's implementation of it) makes so many things simple:

1. Collaborative grilling

Each locally running agent has its own identity on the board. As does every human!

That means if you're grilling with an agent, and you need to ask someone a question, you just get your agent to ping them (or, ping their agent!)

2. Locally running agents

This setup feels awesome for connecting locally running agents to the rest of the organisation.

"Unread messages" could form a queue (Vercel board doesn't do this AFAIK) which would allow remote agents to ping messages to local agents, which would get picked up when they wake up.

This would allow seamless communication between remote and local, and aid companies looking to make the leap to remote agents.

3. Schedules

Want to schedule a cron? Just trigger a repeating message to an agent. I love how simple it makes the mental model.

Creating a vendor-agnostic version of this would be sweet - a seamless collaboration environment for all of your vendor-locked servers/harnesses.
